Hero.label: Healing Nature Trail
Hero.headline: Welcome to <highlight>my trail</highlight>
Hero.subtitle: Luncanilor Plateau, Târsa. A journey toward yourself, guided by the gentle rhythm of nature

Story.label: About me
Story.body1: My name is Oana, I am a mother of two “free range” boys and for over 20 years I have been dancing with the energy of entrepreneurship.
Story.body2: The motto that accompanied me every step along the way has always been the same: "Don't go where the path may lead, go where there is no path and leave a trail"
Story.body3: And that's what I did. I left trails in areas that 'the world' said were impossible or crazy - the first hemp seed processing factory in Europe, cultivation and processing of hemp fibers for the automotive industry, houses made of hemp and lime, a kindergarten in the forest, a democratic free school.
Story.body4: Tourism, real estate, food industry, alternative education, natural constructions, each experience generated a new trail. And only now, after 20 years, have I realised that all these trails actually form a single one, my life.
Story.body5: Today, I want to share everything I have lived and learned, as a certified Healing Nature Guide during gently guided forest bathing sessions in Târsa as well as a facilitator for labyrinth meditations, forest bathing sessions or forest school activities with children at various retreats, festivals or nature oriented team events organised by corporations.

HealingTrail.label: Walden Trail
HealingTrail.title: A journey toward yourself
HealingTrail.body1: The Healing Trail is more than a path through nature, it is a living metaphor for the inner journey.
HealingTrail.body2: Its design is based on interdisciplinary studies, every step on the trail becomes an invitation toward deep connection with yourself through nature. Grounding through the direct contact of your soles with the earth, the experience of touching and listening to flowing water, breathing exercises in the silence of the forest, spaces designed for reflection and introspection.
HealingTrail.body3: And at the decision forks, the trail offers you the choice of unmarked paths, a symbol of adventure, of embracing the unknown, of fresh new perspectives.

Location.label: WHERE TO FIND US
Location.title: Luncanilor Plateau, Târsa
Location.body: The Healing Trail is located in the mountain village of Târsa, Hunedoara county — a place of rare beauty, surrounded by Dacian fortresses and Roman camps, with wide views toward the Orăștie, Apuseni, and Retezat mountains.

Labyrinth.label: A walking meditation
Labyrinth.title: The Labyrinth
Labyrinth.subtitle: The healing walk along a single winding path

what.title: What is a labyrinth?
what.quote: There are many forms of labyrinths all over the world. Some people use them as a tool for prayer, meditation or healing. It is a place where you can gain clarity about your life.
what.intro: A wellness labyrinth is a single winding path that leads, unfailingly, to the centre and back again. No dead ends, no wrong turns. You cannot get lost.
what.vsLabyrinthText: A single path. A sure way to the centre and back.
what.vsMazeText: Many paths, dead ends and the risk of getting lost.

history.title: An ancient practice
history.intro: The labyrinth has been used for over 4,000 years, appearing in many cultures and on every continent.

items.title: The Cretan pattern
items.text: A single path forming seven concentric circuits around the centre — the best-known form being the labyrinth of Knossos.

items.title: The Chartres pattern
items.text: Eleven circuits, made famous by the French cathedral of Chartres. In the Middle Ages, nearly 25% of cathedrals had a labyrinth.

items.title: Nordic stone labyrinths
items.text: Built along the shores of the Baltic Sea, using natural stones set into the ground.

items.title: Tohono O’odham
items.text: “Man in the Maze” — a sacred pattern from Native American tribal art.

why.title: Why walk a labyrinth?
why.quote: The labyrinth is a safe path in uncertain times.
why.cite: Rev. Dr. Lauren Artress, founder of Veriditas
why.text: Walking a labyrinth is a meditation in motion. The pattern holds you while the mind quiets down. Body and breath fall into the same rhythm, and attention gently returns to the present.

stats.title: The healing power of walking
stats.note: Effects reported in a survey of 1,250 people who walked a labyrinth.
stats.quote: The labyrinth teaches us to accept the path and its obstacles, to be in flow with all that is.

effects.title: What happens in body and mind

body.title: In the body
items: Eased muscle tension and chronic pain

steps.title: How to walk a labyrinth
steps.intro: Three simple stages, no experience needed.

items.title: Release
items.text: Enter slowly. Let thoughts and expectations go with each step. Follow the turns without hurrying.

items.title: Receive
items.text: Pause at the centre. Breathe. Stay as long as you like — it is a place for listening.

items.title: Return
items.text: Walk back along the same path, carrying with you the calm and any insights that have emerged.

still.title: For those who find it hard to sit still
still.quote: Many people, like me, have “failed” at sitting meditation. A walking meditation produces the same inner awareness.
still.text: A body in motion gives a restless mind something to do. Attention settles on the path, the breath, the steps — and the meditative state arises on its own.
still.videoCaption: The mobile labyrinth, brought to retreats and team-building events

where.title: Where we can build a labyrinth
where.intro: Labyrinths can be built in town squares, parks, office buildings, urban gardens and quiet corners of the forest.

items.title: In the forest
items.text: A perfect companion for forest bathing and time spent in nature.

items.title: Urban spaces
items.text: A quiet way to pause and recentre yourself in the midst of a busy life.

items.title: Garden labyrinths
items.text: Marked out with stones, string or simply mown into the grass.

items.title: The Chartres pattern
items.text: The medieval design, still walked as a mini-pilgrimage at the cathedral near Paris.

finger.title: Finger labyrinths for meditation at home
finger.text: The same winding path in miniature: trace it with a finger, eyes closed. If you would like one, get in touch.
finger.cta: Contact me if you want one

Journal.label: A 21-day journal
Journal.title: Sit Spot Journal
Journal.subtitle: The Practice of Returning
Journal.lead: What if, for 21 days, you had a date with yourself?
list: Not with everything you “have” to do.
paragraphs: Just you, a spot in nature, and a few minutes to observe, breathe, feel, and write.

“Sit Spot or The Practice of Returning” is more than just a journal. It is an invitation for the one who feels that, amidst all errands run for others, it might be time to take a journey one toward oneself.

For 21 days, you return to the same spot with a bit of nature – under a tree, in a corner of a garden, along a path – and begin to notice things you may have passed by hundreds of times before without ever seeing. You write. You sketch. You wonder. Sometimes, perhaps, you write nothing at all. And that is perfectly fine.
Because the goal is not to fill up pages.
Journal.emphasis: The goal is simply to be there.
closing: This journal was born from a desire to bring a bit of the forest’s tranquility into the city – into everyone’s own backyard – so that you might experience a return to nature, to simplicity, to presence, and, perhaps most importantly, a return to yourself.
Because sometimes, we don’t need yet another answer. We need a little bit of stillness to hear the answer that was already within us.
